conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’re checking a stool test for C. diff—Clostridium difficile—because it can cause nausea and gut issues, especially after antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve had that before! That was awful. Please don’t let it come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. We also did a chest X-ray today because we heard some wheezing. It looked stable—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My heart’s not great either. EF was 40% last time. Is my fluid okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs have some rales, but we think it’s manageable. You’re scheduled for dialysis tomorrow to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood sugar? I’m always worried about lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had two episodes of low blood sugar overnight. We’ve reduced your evening insulin dose to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I hate feeling shaky and confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff. That’s likely what caused your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. So it’s back. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history. But we’re stopping the IV antibiotic and starting you on oral vancomycin, which treats C. diff well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take metronidazole, right? I couldn’t keep it down last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re using vancomycin. You’ll take it four times a day for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Foley? Should we change it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we changed it yesterday. Even though the urine culture was contaminated, we didn’t want to risk a real infection on top of C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smart. My white count is high—12.6. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s elevated, but it was even higher in the ER. It’s coming down since we started treatment, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? Creatinine is 3.6 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. With ESRD, it fluctuates. Dialysis will help clear it. We’re continuing your phosphate binders and nephrocaps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my heart meds? I know I’ve been skipping carvedilol when I feel bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it on board. You got IV metoprolol when your BP spiked, but we want you on oral carvedilol long-term for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. The dizziness scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor. Your blood pressure has been high, but it’s better now that you’re feeling less nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest labs show your white count is still high but stable. You’re responding to the vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any fever? I felt warm last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your max temperature was 100.9—slightly elevated, but not concerning. Blood cultures came back negative, so no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. So it’s just the C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’re treating it appropriately. You’re feeling better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Nausea is gone. I even ate some toast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I take the vancomycin at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for two weeks. We’ll send it with you. Also, ondansetron for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? You changed it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered your glargine to 2 units morning and night to prevent lows. The sliding scale stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain meds? I’ve been using the oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue both the long-acting and immediate-release oxycodone as needed. Gabapentin is still on board for nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I have that phantom pain in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We haven’t changed your pain regimen. The lidocaine patch and dilaudid are still available if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. You’ll go home with services to help with nursing and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to go. Just want to stay out of the hospital for a while!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Remember: finish all the vancomycin, watch for diarrhea, and call if you feel sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled. We’ll send all the records. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. You and the team were great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in because of anemia and blood in your stool, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I didn’t actually see the blood myself. My sister said she noticed it about a week ago. I’ve been feeling fine otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your hemoglobin was quite low when you came in—down to 6.3 from your usual mid-30s. That’s why we gave you one unit of blood in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh wow, that’s a big drop. Is that from the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. It’s likely a slow, chronic bleed. We’re not sure exactly where it’s coming from yet, but we’ll check with a colonoscopy soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff before—could that be causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, C. diff colitis can sometimes cause bleeding. You’re already on oral vancomycin for it, which we’ll continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I couldn’t tolerate the metronidazole last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. You’ll stay on vancomycin. We also placed a central line in your right subclavian vein because we couldn’t get regular IV access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that. It was uncomfortable, but I understand why it was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you some pain medicine for that. Your vitals are stable now, and your lungs are clear. We’ll keep monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just hungry. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need to stay NPO—nothing by mouth—until after your colonoscopy tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I hope I can eat soon. I’m used to my insulin schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Lantus insulin twice daily and sliding scale as needed. We’ll adjust it once you’re eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Hemoglobin went up to 7.9 after the transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When’s the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later this morning. We’ll also do an upper endoscopy to check your stomach and upper GI tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both? I thought it was a lower GI issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but since we’re not sure of the source, we want to check everything. Better safe than sorry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The colonoscopy is done. You have internal hemorrhoids, but otherwise the colon looks normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hemorrhoids? Could that be the source of the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The GI team thinks it could be from the hemorrhoids or your C. diff. The upper endoscopy was completely normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no ulcers or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, everything looked healthy up there. We’ll keep monitoring your hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can start with clear liquids. We’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is holding steady at 9.5. We’re giving you a second unit of blood today to help rebuild your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal? Two units?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given how low it was, yes. Your body just needs time to recover. Blood cultures were negative, so no sign of infection in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough infections lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also checking for other causes of anemia—iron, B12, folate. All came back normal, so it’s likely blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is now 10.1. That’s a good improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure you’re stable and not bleeding. We also switched your heart medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on carvedilol. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of the low blood pressure after the bleed, we switched you to metoprolol, which is gentler. We’ll restart aspirin before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as my heart’s protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Hemoglobin is stable at 10.1. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need more tests after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team said no follow-up scopes are needed. Just keep an eye on your stool and let your PCP know if you see blood again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my C. diff treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the oral vancomycin as prescribed. Watch for diarrhea or cramps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your session yesterday. Continue with your regular schedule. We’ll keep your phosphate binder and Nephrocaps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your medications as listed, especially the vancomycin, metoprolol, and insulin. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week to check your blood count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel weak or see blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back right away. Otherwise, you’re doing well. We’ll send instructions to your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You were brought in because you were unresponsive this morning. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember taking my insulin and eating breakfast. Then I got really dizzy and don’t remember much after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was very low—only 16. That’s why you passed out. We gave you dextrose through your dialysis line and you woke up. Did you take more insulin than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took my usual sliding scale. My sugar was 147, so I took my normal dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We looked at your records and it seems like you may have taken more than needed. A sugar of 147 usually only needs 2 units. Taking more could have caused the low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I must have misread. I’ve been so tired lately, it’s hard to focus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re also concerned about your blood pressure. It dropped to 78 over 40. We gave you fluids and it’s better now, but we think you might be dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much. My stomach’s been off since I left the hospital a few days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had diarrhea before, right? We tested your stool and it came back positive for C. diff—Clostridium difficile. That can cause dehydration and weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I just had that last time. Why does it keep coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your medical history—diabetes, dialysis, and multiple antibiotics—it’s easier for C. diff to return. We’re starting you on oral vancomycin again, but on a longer taper to try to prevent another relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. But will it make me feel better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help over the next few days. We also need to watch for infection. Your urine looked cloudy and had some bacteria, so we started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a catheter, so my urine’s always messy. Is it really an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’re not sure yet. We’ll wait for the culture. If it’s just contamination, we’ll stop the antibiotics. But with your history of resistant infections, we had to start them just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was on strong antibiotics and got sicker. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Right now, you don’t have fever or signs of sepsis, so we may stop them soon. We don’t want to over-treat, especially with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My heart’s been racing too. Is that from the low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You did have tachycardia earlier, but your EKG was normal. It could also be from dehydration. We’ll keep an eye on it. You have heart failure, so we want to make sure your heart’s not stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. My ejection fraction is 40%, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. We had to hold your blood pressure meds temporarily because your pressure was low, but we’ll restart them as you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I don’t want another low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on a sliding scale, but we’ll monitor your sugars closely. They’ve been in the 150–200 range, which is safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m just so tired all the time. Is it the anemia again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low—9.1—but it’s stable from your last admission. We don’t think you’re actively bleeding. It’s likely from your kidney disease. We won’t need a transfusion this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my dialysis? I’m due tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll have dialysis tomorrow. We’ll do it at bedside since you’re still unstable for transport. We’re using your dialysis line for fluids too, since we couldn’t get regular IV access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t want a central line. That’s why I said no.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respected that. Using your dialysis line was a safe alternative. It’s helping us give you fluids and meds without another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It showed gram-negative rods, but in low numbers. We think it’s not a true infection, so we’re stopping the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a UTI? I’m glad. I was worried about another resistant bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With your history of MDR organisms like Klebsiella, we had to be cautious. But no signs of sepsis, and your vitals are stable, so we’re de-escalating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the C. diff? Is the vancomycin working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it to. You’ve had three episodes, so we’re using a tapered course—starting high and slowly reducing—to reduce the chance of recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it as long as I need to. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you. Also, your blood pressure is better—110 over 70—so we’re restarting your metoprolol today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And aspirin? I was on that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue aspirin for heart protection. We’re not sure why you weren’t on a statin, but we’ll discuss that with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your blood pressure and heart rate are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your labs are stable, and your mental status is back to baseline. The plan is to replace your dialysis catheter this afternoon—it’s been in a while and could be a source of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it for months. Is it safe to change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the transplant team will do it. It’s routine. We’re doing it before you go home to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust them. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping calcium acetate—it’s not needed right now. And we’re switching from trazodone to mirtazapine for sleep. It’s gentler on your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was having nightmares on trazodone. I’m glad to stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mirtazapine might help with both sleep and appetite. You’ve lost weight, and we want you to regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter was replaced successfully. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. Still tired, but not dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Keep taking the vancomycin for the full course, even if you feel fine. Stopping early can cause relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my gabapentin? It’s not helping my nerve pain much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP can increase it gradually. We’ve noted that in your discharge instructions. Start slow to avoid dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll call them right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re alert, your vitals are stable, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: finish the vancomycin, take mirtazapine at night, and follow up with your PCP about your pain and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll be more careful with my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Call if you feel dizzy, have diarrhea, or your sugars go too low. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I started having swelling on the right side of my face, and my tongue felt like it was swelling too. I had trouble breathing at first, but that’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was this sudden? Any fever, rash, or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It came on fast. No fever or pain, but I was really scared. I think it might be from that new antidepressant—mirtazipine. I started it right before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We gave you some medications in the ER—diphenhydramine, prednisone, and famotidine—to help with the swelling. We’re thinking this might be angioedema, which can happen with certain medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Angioedema? I’ve never heard of that. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially if the throat or tongue swells a lot. But you’re breathing fine now, and there’s no stridor, so we’re not worried about your airway. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your swelling. We also did blood tests and a chest X-ray. The X-ray looked clear—no pneumonia or fluid. Your labs show mild inflammation, but nothing alarming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? I haven’t taken my Lantus since last time—I got so low, I passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re keeping you on the sliding scale insulin for now. We’ll talk to your endocrinologist about adjusting your long-acting insulin safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And I’m still on that vancomycin for C. diff, right? I haven’t had diarrhea, but I don’t want it coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re continuing the vancomycin taper as planned. No signs of infection now, so we’re staying the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been through that too many times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep your other meds—metoprolol, aspirin, gabapentin, and oxycodone—for your heart, pain, and nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis? I’m due soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get dialysis tomorrow as scheduled. Your kidney function is stable, so we’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. So this swelling—it’s really from the mirtazipine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely. Mirtazipine can cause angioedema in rare cases. We checked your complement levels—C3 and C4—and they’re mostly normal, so it’s not a genetic form. Stopping the mirtazipine should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I shouldn’t take it anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we recommend stopping it. Talk to your psychiatrist about a different antidepressant when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the prednisone—I’m supposed to keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 20 mg daily for five more days. It helps reduce the swelling and prevent it from coming back quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can raise blood sugar, so we’ll monitor that. Also, don’t stop it suddenly—tapering helps avoid withdrawal symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My sugar’s already high—I saw 438 in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s from the stress and steroids. We’ll adjust your insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my urine? I always have bacteria, but ID said not to treat it last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You have chronic colonization from the catheter. No signs of infection now, so we’re not treating it. Antibiotics could make C. diff worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I don’t need more pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your face looks much better—swelling is nearly gone. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can see both eyes now! No tongue swelling either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll discharge you today. Keep taking the prednisone for five days, and don’t restart mirtazipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And dialysis is scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re set for tomorrow. Your home nurse will help with insulin and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the swelling comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have any trouble breathing or swelling in your throat, go to the ER immediately. Otherwise, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I feel a lot safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your primary team knows about the mirtazipine. Take care, and follow up with your doctors soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
